title: Juan Diego (9 December)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas, the bishop at the window with a bag of gold. Your line was in secret.

Birdsong, before sunrise, on a bare hill called Tepeyac, which today lies inside Mexico City. An Indigenous man named Juan Diego is walking past on his way to church when the singing stops him. Then a woman's voice calls him by name, gently, the way you'd call a child. He climbs toward it and finds a Lady standing on the hill, shining. She has an errand for him: go to the bishop and ask that a church be built right here. She has picked her messenger.
screen: `BIRDSONG ON TEPEYAC.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `GO TO THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Nican Mopohua, an account written in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. The first surprise is how the Lady talks to him. She uses tender forms: my littlest one, my youngest child. The Nahuatl word is noxocoyouh. Juan Diego goes to the bishop, waits, and is politely doubted. He comes back and does something very human: he asks her to send someone else. In the account he calls himself a nobody, small, not the kind of man bishops listen to. Please, send someone important. She refuses. She has plenty of messengers, she says, but it's him she wants. Then his uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, running for a priest, takes a different path around the hill so he won't have to face her and explain. She comes down and meets him anyway. She tells him his uncle is already well, and asks, in effect, whether he has forgotten that she is his mother and he is under her care. Then she sends him up the hill to gather flowers, in a season when nothing should be blooming. He carries them to the bishop folded in his tilma, his cloak. He opens it, the flowers fall, and on the cloth is the image of the Lady that pilgrims still visit at Guadalupe. Mary's own song in Luke says it plainly. In the Douay-Rheims: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble." The bishop needed a sign. It came in the hands of the man who thought he didn't count.
screen: `MY LITTLEST ONE: NOXOCOYOUH.` · `PLEASE, SEND SOMEONE IMPORTANT.` · `HE TAKES THE OTHER PATH; SHE FINDS HIM.` · `FLOWERS, A CLOAK, AN IMAGE.` · then, large: `AND HATH EXALTED THE HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who bring things to you and are rarely noticed: the mail carrier, the delivery driver, the person who cleans the building after everyone leaves. Choose one face, and remember one thing they've carried to you. If you pray, thank God for them by name, or by their job if you don't know the name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude.
Juan Diego. The Indigenous man of Tepeyac who asked to be replaced by someone important, and was chosen anyway, his cloak full of flowers.
Your line: the littlest son. She had plenty of messengers, and she wanted him. Day one thousand fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: Saint Juan Diego is remembered on 9 December, shortly before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims visit the basilica at Tepeyac, where the tilma is kept, especially in those days.

notes: Original: confirm the spelling and pronunciation of 'noxocoyouh' (my youngest child) as it appears in the Nican Mopohua, and its gloss. If uncertain, replace with the Lady's form of address 'Juantzin, Juan Diegotzin'.

All story details (birdsong, the request for a church, the bishop's doubt, Juan Diego asking her to send someone important, the detour around the hill, the uncle's healing, the flowers in winter, the image on the tilma) are paraphrased from the Nican Mopohua; confirm.
The Lady's 'Am I not here, I who am your mother?' is paraphrased ('whether he has forgotten that she is his mother'), since no public-domain English translation is cited.
Years (1531 apparitions, 2002 canonization), the bishop's name (Zumárraga) and the Castilian roses are left out under the claims rule.
'Pilgrims still visit at Guadalupe': confirm phrasing.
Audit: hook said Tepeyac was 'outside what is now Mexico City'; the hill lies within today's Mexico City (it was outside the old city), so the line now says so.
Editor pass: the count 'three days before' the Guadalupe feast in howItsDone changed to 'shortly before' under the claims rule; script otherwise unchanged.
